title: Platform systems & services: how-tos, dashboards, alerts, runbooks, retro, and roadmap
author: Arjun Patel
content:
Summary:
This page consolidates the platform team's canonical guidance for systems and services: standard how-tos, dashboard and alert ownership, primary runbooks, retrospective cadence and templates, and the near-term roadmap. Use this as the single entry point for operational changes that affect dashboards, alerts, or on-call behavior.

Goals:
- Reduce alert noise by 40% year over year through standardized alert levels and runbook-driven automation.
- Ensure runbooks are actionable and testable: every high-severity alert must have a <60s runbook verification test.
- Keep dashboards focused on ownerable SLOs and top failure modes to speed troubleshooting.

Table of contents:
1) Overview and ownership
2) How-tos: creating dashboards and managed panels
3) Alerts: levels, thresholds, and tuning playbook
4) Runbooks: structure and canonical steps
5) Retrospective & blameless review template
6) Roadmap (next 6 months)
7) Team wiki hygiene and governance
8) Appendix: alert config table, PromQL examples, escalation contacts

1) Overview and ownership
- Scope: platform core services (kube control plane, infra provisioning API, service mesh, shared caches, logging pipeline, and the platform control plane services). For product-facing model serving endpoints see eng-serving-runtime.
- Owners: Each service MUST have a primary and secondary owner defined in the service README and registered in the oncall rota system.
  - Platform core infra: owner: infra-team@redwood.com (primary: Priya Rao, secondary: Marcus Alvarez)
  - Observability stack: owner: eng-platform-observability@redwood.com (primary: Lina Chen)
  - Service mesh / ingress: owner: networking@redwood.com (primary: Aisha Ndlovu)
- SLOs and indicators: all services must publish a 3-tier SLO (availability / p99 latency / error budget burn). Dashboard panels must surface real-time burn rate and 7d trend.

2) How-tos: creating dashboards and managed panels
Intro: Dashboards should be diagnostic, not exploratory. A canonical dashboard contains: Overview (healthy/unhealthy), Key SLO panels, Top error modes, Recent incidents list.
Step-by-step:
1. Duplicate the team dashboard template (confluence link: /dashboards/templates/platform-team-template).
2. Add owner metadata at the top of the dashboard: owner, escalation policy, last updated.
3. Add panels:
   - SLO availability (0-1): query -> service_availability{svc=~"<svc>"}
   - p99 latency: query -> histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
   - error rate: sum(rate(request_errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m]))
4. Validate queries in panel preview. Ensure panel load time < 500ms in Grafana.
5. Submit a dashboard change PR in observability repo. Tag reviewers: observability, owner.
6. After merge, run the dashboard smoke test: visit the dashboard URL and run the `dashboard-smoke` job (CI): `make smoke-dashboard ARGS="--dashboard-id <id>"`.
Best practices:
- Keep dashboards to a single owner.
- Limit panels: prefer 6-10 key panels per screen.
- Use variable filters sparingly (service, region, cluster).

3) Alerts: levels, thresholds, and tuning playbook
Alert levels and expected response times:
- Sev-P0 (Pager, immediate): Service Unavailable affecting >5% of requests OR control plane outage. Response goal: 15 minutes.
- Sev-P1 (Pager, high): SLO breach in progress or error budget burn > 10% in 1h. Response goal: 30 minutes.
- Sev-P2 (Email/Slack, medium): Degraded latency (p99 > target * 2) for >10 minutes. Response goal: 4 hours.
- Sev-P3 (Ticket): Low priority anomalies or single-user issues. Response goal: next-sprint remediation.
Alert content requirements (required on every alert):
- Short description (1 line)
- Impact (who/what is affected)
- Owner (team/contact)
- Runbook link (runbooks/<runbook-id>)
- Suggested actions (2 bullets)
Tuning playbook (what to do when an alert fires repeatedly):
1. If alert fires > 3 times/day, reduce sensitivity: increase evaluation window or threshold by 20%.
2. If the alert indicates a new failure mode, open an incident and add to the next retro.
3. If suppression is required, use a temporary mute with a linked Jira and owner.

4) Runbooks: structure and canonical steps
Every runbook must include (top to bottom):
- Title, service, owner, last tested date, severity mapped to alert IDs
- Impact summary and how to detect the problem
- Pre-checks (what to look for first)
- Step-by-step remediation actions (numbered)
- Rollback or mitigation options (if applicable)
- Post-incident validation (how to confirm service recovered)
- Post-incident tasks (follow up items, config changes, PRs)
Example (Kubernetes control plane high etcd latency):
1. Confirm symptoms: etcd_request_duration_seconds p95 > 500ms for 5m.
2. Find high-load pods: kubectl top pods -n kube-system | sort -nr -k3
3. If disk pressure, run `kubectl drain` targeted nodes to migrate control plane consumers.
4. If etcd leader flapping, collect diagnostics: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:2379/health | jq .; gather logs `journalctl -u etcd -n 500` and upload to incident artifact store.
5. If no immediate resolution, fail over to passive etcd replica following the etcd failover doc (link).
Testing runbooks:
- Every runbook must have a quarterly test date and recorded outcome in the runbook header. Tests are scoped to non-production early Monday slack windows.

5) Retrospective & blameless review template
Cadence: for Sev-P0/P1 incidents, run a retro within 7 business days. For recurring P2 events add to monthly reliability retro.
Retro template (to be filled in the incident doc):
- Incident summary (what, when, impact)
- Timeline (concise timeboxed steps)
- Root cause analysis (primary and contributing factors)
- What went well (responses, mitigations)
- What to improve (process, tooling, runbook gaps)
- Action items (owner, due date, verification criteria)
- Postmortem follow up: link to PRs and config changes; verify closure when all action items pass smoke tests.
Blameless rules:
- Focus on systems and process causes, not individuals.
- Seek to fix systems that allow human error to recur.

6) Roadmap (next 6 months)
Milestones and owners:
- Q3 2026: Alert standardization sprint: standardize severities and update 120 alerts across platform (owner: Lina Chen).
- Q4 2026: Dashboard modernization: migrate team dashboards to new templating system with improved caching (owner: Observability team, lead Marcus Alvarez).
- Q4 2026: Runbook automation: add CI smoke tests for top 30 runbooks (owner: eng-platform).
- Q1 2027: Auto-remediation pilot: safe auto-rollback for common transient failures (owner: automation squad).
Roadmap principles:
- Prioritize work that reduces time-to-restore and repetitive manual toil.
- Measure success via incident MTTR, alert noise (alerts per week), and % of runbooks with test coverage.

7) Team wiki hygiene and governance
- Naming conventions: `service-name/owner/dashboard` and `runbooks/service-name/runbook-title.md`.
- Ownership enforcement: every merged PR that touches alerts or dashboards must include `observability-approval` and list a primary owner in the PR description.
- Documentation lifecycle: owners must review their dashboards and runbooks quarterly. A stale badge is added automatically if last_updated > 90 days.

8) Appendix: alert config table, PromQL examples, escalation contacts
Alert config (canonical table):
| Alert ID | Severity | Condition (summary) | Owner | Pager? | Escalation window | Recovery check |
|---------|----------|---------------------|-------|--------|-------------------|----------------|
| PLAT_CTRLPLANE_DOWN | P0 | control plane unavailable > 2m | infra-team@redwood.com | Yes | 15m escalate to oncall lead | `service_availability > 0.05`
| OBS_GRAFANA_SLOW | P2 | grafana panel render > 2s | observability@redwood.com | No | 4h create ticket | panel render time < 1s
| LOG_PIPE_ERRORS_HIGH | P1 | log pipeline error rate > 3% (5m) | logging-team@redwood.com | Yes | 30m | error rate < 1% for 10m

PromQL snippets (examples):
- Error rate: `sum(rate(request_errors_total{service=\"svc-a\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total{service=\"svc-a\"}[5m]))`
- P99 latency: `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))`
- SLO breach burn rate: `increase(slo_burn_total{service=\"svc-a\",slo=\"availability\"}[1h]) / 3600`

Escalation contacts:
- Platform oncall Slack: #oncall-platform (primary pager)
- Observability lead: Lina Chen / lina@redwood.com
- Infra lead: Priya Rao / priya@redwood.com
- Oncall manager: ops-manager@redwood.com

Change process (alerts/dashboards/runbooks):
1. Open a change PR in `observability` repo with a description, owner, and test plan.
2. Tag `observability` and `service owner` for review.
3. Run CI smoke tests (dashboard-smoke / runbook-smoke).
4. After 48h post-merge, review metrics for alert flapping; if noise increases, revert and iterate.

Appendix: Links and artifacts
- Dashboard templates: /dashboards/templates/platform-team-template
- Runbook repo: git@github.com:redwood/platform-runbooks.git
- Incident doc template: /incidents/templates/sev-p0-template
- Roadmap board: /boards/platform-roadmap

Notes and governance reminders:
- Major changes to alert severity or automatic muting require an RFC and owner signoff.
- We prioritize small, reversible changes.
- If you're unsure which severity to choose, default to P2 and escalate after post-merge monitoring.

If you have questions or want a walkthrough of the dashboard/change process, book time with the observability pod via the platform calendar.
